Getting started with layaR

Source: vignettes/layaR.Rmd
layaR.Rmd

layaR runs Laya decision models on your own machine. You ask typed questions about a piece of text (a support ticket, an email, a chat message, a prompt) and get calibrated answers back:

  • choice: pick one label from a fixed set of options;
  • score: place the text on an ordinal scale;
  • noul (yes/no): the probability that a statement holds.

All the questions about one text are answered in a single forward pass, so asking five questions costs about as much as asking one. Prediction runs on the CPU through ONNX Runtime; no Python, server or API key is involved.

Getting a model

layaR needs an ONNX export of a Laya checkpoint. Download one once (1.3 to 1.6 GB):

library(layaR)
laya_download_model("multilingual")

There are three checkpoints:

Checkpoint Base encoder Use it for
multilingual mmBERT-base text in any of 100+ languages (the default)
english ModernBERT-large English text; slightly more accurate there
typed-decisions ModernBERT-large four specific workflows it was fine-tuned on

laya_models() shows what is installed:

library(layaR)
m <- laya_models()
m$path <- sub(path.expand("~"), "~", m$path, fixed = TRUE)
m
#>        checkpoint installed                                  path source layout size_gb
#> 1    multilingual      TRUE    ~/.cache/R/layaR/onnx/multilingual  layaR  fused    1.32
#> 2         english      TRUE         ~/.cache/R/layaR/onnx/english  layaR  fused    1.69
#> 3 typed-decisions      TRUE ~/.cache/R/layaR/onnx/typed-decisions  layaR  fused    1.69

vignette("models-and-performance", package = "layaR") covers where models live, importing your own export, memory and threads.

Asking questions

Build a question set with laya_questions(). Each named argument is one question, and the name becomes the answer’s id:

questions <- laya_questions(
  department = laya_choice(
    "Which department should handle this request?",
    billing   = "invoices, payments, refunds",
    technical = "bugs, outages, system errors",
    sales     = "pricing, new contracts",
    other     = "everything else"
  ),
  urgency = laya_score(
    "How urgent is this request?",
    c("not urgent", "soon", "critical deadline or blocking issue")
  ),
  churn_risk = laya_noul("Does the user threaten to cancel or leave?")
)
questions
#> <laya_questions> 3 questions
#>   department  choice Which department should handle this request?  [4 options: billing, technical, sales, other]
#>   urgency     score  How urgent is this request?  [3 levels]
#>   churn_risk  noul   Does the user threaten to cancel or leave?  [yes/no]

A state is the text the model reads. It can be a single string, or a named list whose field names give the model context:

state <- list(
  subject = "Duplicate charge on invoice #4411",
  body = paste("Hi, we were billed twice for March.",
               "Please refund the duplicate today or we will cancel our plan.")
)

laya_predict() answers every question at once. The first call loads the model, which takes a few seconds; the engine is then kept for the session.

res <- laya_predict(state, questions)
res
#> <laya_result> laya-rl-agent · 3 answers · 234 input tokens
#>   department  choice  billing        p 1.00  confidence 1.00
#>   urgency     score   1.87 (0–2)    confidence 0.64
#>   churn_risk  noul    0.04 → FALSE  confidence 0.96

Two of the answers are right: the ticket is for billing, and it is fairly urgent. The third is wrong. The message ends with “or we will cancel our plan”, yet the model puts the probability of a cancellation threat at 0.04, with confidence 0.96. A conditional threat phrased as a request is the kind of wording yes/no questions can miss.

It is a useful reminder: confidence is calibrated on the data the checkpoints were trained on, not on yours, and a confident answer can still be wrong. Before acting on answers automatically, check a few dozen labelled examples from your own workflow.

When a question misses, reword it. Here the word “threaten” is the problem; asking whether the customer says they will cancel gets it right:

reworded <- laya_questions(churn_risk = laya_noul("Does the customer say they will cancel or leave?"))
laya_predict(state, reworded)
#> <laya_result> laya-rl-agent · 1 answer · 76 input tokens
#>   churn_risk  noul    0.88 → TRUE   confidence 0.88

vignette("writing-questions", package = "layaR") has more on wording.

Reading the answers

as.data.frame() gives one row per question:

as.data.frame(res)
#>           id   type  answer  value confidence answer_confidence act_probability
#> 1 department choice billing 1.0000     1.0000            1.0000               1
#> 2    urgency  score    1.87 1.8685     0.6371            0.8721               1
#> 3 churn_risk   noul   FALSE 0.0360     0.9640            0.9640               1
#>   abstention
#> 1       <NA>
#> 2       <NA>
#> 3       <NA>
  • answer is the label for a choice question, the expected level for a score question (here between 0, “not urgent”, and 2, “critical”), and TRUE/FALSE for a yes/no question.
  • value is the chosen label’s probability, the score, or P(true).
  • confidence is how sure the model is of its answer, from 0 to 1. The checkpoints are calibrated: across many answers given with confidence 0.8, about 80% are right.

laya_probabilities() shows the whole distribution, one row per option:

laya_probabilities(res)
#>           id   type                              option probability
#> 1 department choice                             billing      1.0000
#> 2 department choice                           technical      0.0000
#> 3 department choice                               sales      0.0000
#> 4 department choice                               other      0.0000
#> 5    urgency  score                          not urgent      0.0036
#> 6    urgency  score                                soon      0.1243
#> 7    urgency  score critical deadline or blocking issue      0.8721
#> 8 churn_risk   noul                               false      0.9640
#> 9 churn_risk   noul                                true      0.0360

The result is also a plain list in the Python SDK’s shape, so you can reach into it directly:

res$answers$department$choice
#> [1] "billing"
res$answers$churn_risk$noul
#> [1] 0.036

When the model isn’t sure

Set min_confidence and every answer reports whether it passed the threshold. An abstained answer is still there; it is flagged so you can send it to a person instead:

vague <- "Hi, quick question about my account."
as.data.frame(laya_predict(vague, questions, min_confidence = 0.8))[
  , c("id", "answer", "confidence", "abstention")]
#>           id  answer confidence abstention
#> 1 department billing     0.1485  abstained
#> 2    urgency    1.78     0.4988  abstained
#> 3 churn_risk   FALSE     0.9966     passed

Presets

Five ready-made question sets come from the Python SDK. Each reads one field of the state:

laya_preset_fields()
#>       preset state_field
#> 1     triage     message
#> 2      email        body
#> 3      guard      prompt
#> 4 moderation        post
#> 5     router     request
laya_predict(list(message = "My payment failed twice and nobody answers my emails!"),
             laya_preset("triage"))
#> <laya_result> laya-rl-agent · 5 answers · 321 input tokens
#>   intent            choice  billing_quest… p 0.99  confidence 0.97
#>   is_urgent         noul    0.01 → FALSE  confidence 0.99
#>   frustration       score   1.99 (0–3)    confidence 0.17
#>   refund_requested  noul    0.02 → FALSE  confidence 0.98
#>   churn_risk        noul    0.00 → FALSE  confidence 1.00
